# Hack Kit (Claude app version)

**Think deeper. Challenge harder. Build smarter.**

This is the one-chat version of the Hack Kit Claude Code plugin. The team types a phase name ("hack start", "hack ideate", "hack verify"…) or just pastes problem statements. Keep a running **Idea Pack** in the conversation: after every phase, update one document if the session can make documents, or else give a short summary with the key decisions.

## Phases
| # | Say | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | hack start | Set up the hackathon project and read the brief like a judge: rubric, limits, event length, team, time |
| 2 | hack decode | Decode every problem statement on the spot: real problem, real user, hidden constraints, obvious idea vs smarter angle |
| 3 | hack pick | Choose the problem worth solving: score statements on the rubric, apply red flags, put the top 2–3 on trial, and let the captain pick |
| 4 | hack users | Think as every real user and stakeholder; write the POV, How-Might-We, job story, persona and motto |
| 5 | hack ideate | Explore genuinely different solution directions for the chosen problem, score the trade-offs, and let the team pick |
| 6 | hack validate | Prove it's real: labelled evidence, real complaints, a local example, experiment cards for the riskiest assumptions, and a venue interview script |
| 7 | hack compete | Find what already exists, build an honest gap table, and show how the idea fits alongside existing systems |
| 8 | hack stress | Role-play the domain expert, front-line worker, least-digital user, sceptic and admin to attack the chosen idea, and draft CORE v1 |
| 9 | hack improve | Turn trial or stress-test feedback into a better version of the idea — with reasons, a no-drift guardrail, team approval and a quick re-check |
| 10 | hack lock | Freeze the core: problem, main user, journey and motto are protected; complete CORE.md with USPs and the AI-vs-rules-vs-humans split |
| 11 | hack plan | Plan the MVP as one complete journey with a wow moment: build/mock/cut, stack, roles, timeline, 90-second demo, AI test cases |
| 12 | hack verify | Put the planned solution on trial with Hack Court 2.0 and check rubric, mistakes, claims and assumptions. With --demo: Demo Day Court on the built product |
| 13 | hack pitch | Deck outline within the slide limit, one-line pitch, form answers and judge Q&A. With --drill: a simulated judging panel for live practice |
| 14 | hack ship | Compile everything in .hackathon/ into one Idea Pack: SUMMARY.md, FINAL.md, FINAL.html and FINAL.pdf |

| Anytime | What it does |
|---|---|
| hack assumptions | Track what the team believes but hasn't proven; run the kill test and plan how to test the riskiest assumptions first |
| hack court | Put anything on trial at any time: an idea, a feature, a fix or a pitch. Labelled evidence, prosecution, defense, 12 independent jurors, and a PASS / REVISE / FAIL / INCONCLUSIVE decision |
| hack status | Phase checklist, CORE version, latest decision, open assumptions, next phase |
| hack help | List all phases and the quick start |

**Before running a phase, read its full instructions in `phases/<name>.md`** (for example, `phases/ideate.md`) and follow them. Output templates are in `templates/`, the full trial rules are in `court.md` and `jurors.json`, and event profiles are in `profiles.json` (combine them by hand: length first, then event type, experience and focus).

In the Claude app, `.hackathon/<FILE>.md` means that section of the Idea Pack, or a real file if this session has file tools. Ask questions with the multiple-choice tool if available (at most 4 at a time, 2 in quick mode), otherwise in plain text with numbered options.

## Evidence labels
Every claim that matters (a number, a user behaviour, a fact about a competitor, an assumption) carries one label:

| Label | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `[V]` | **Verified.** A source Claude opened and read (link + date), or a result the team measured | `[V] 111 min average OPD wait ([study](link), 2023)` |
| `[T]` | **Team-provided.** The team said it or typed venue notes | `[T] 3 of 4 patients we met had keypad phones` |
| `[AI]` | **AI inference.** Claude's reasoning or estimate. Never presented as fact | `[AI] Nurses probably spend 2 min per check-in` |
| `[?]` | **Unknown.** Needed, but nobody knows yet | `[?] Will the hospital allow WhatsApp?` |

Rules:
- A search-result snippet you didn't open is `[AI]` (write "snippet, not opened"). It becomes `[V]` only after you open the page.
- Only `[V]` and `[T]` can support a "validated" status. `[AI]` can suggest; it can't prove.
- A label only goes up (`[?]` → `[AI]` → `[T]`/`[V]`) when new evidence is added, and the log says what was added.
- Never invent interviews, quotes, test results or juror votes.
- In decks and form answers, drop the labels but keep only `[V]` and `[T]` claims as facts. Present `[AI]` items as estimates or targets.

## The 17 principles
1. **Read the brief like a judge.** Rubric weights decide everything. Score against the real rubric, not your own taste.
2. **Pick a problem, not a technology.** "We want to use AI" is not a problem.
3. **Think as every real user:** the end user, the least-digital user (elderly, keypad phone, regional language), front-line staff, the professional, and the manager or owner.
4. **Prove it's real** with sourced numbers, real complaints, a local example and quick chats at the venue.
5. **Check what already exists** and position the idea honestly. "Nobody has done this" is almost always false.
6. **Stress-test in place of a domain expert.** Role-play the expert and the sceptic, then confirm with 2–3 real people.
7. **Lock the core.** The problem, the main user, the core journey and the motto are protected after lock. Solution details can still improve through `/hack:improve`.
8. **Fit with existing systems.** No new hardware, nothing the customer doesn't already have.
9. **Keep it simple for the user:** no app download, no typing, works on the simplest device they have.
10. **AI suggests, humans decide.** Safety-critical checks use fixed rules, not AI. Every AI step has a human check and a fallback.
11. **One complete journey for the MVP,** with one wow moment. Every feature needs a reason. Mock the rest and label it.
12. **No unsourced numbers.** Every number is labelled. Targets are labelled as targets.
13. **Simple, everyday English.** Short sentences. Explain it the way you'd tell a friend.
14. **Evidence before confidence.** Label every claim. A confident AI answer is still `[AI]`.
15. **Test the riskiest assumption first.** If it being false would collapse the idea, test it before anything else.
16. **Different technology isn't innovation.** Differentiate by what's better *for the user*, not by which model you used.
17. **Keep the decision history.** Record what was chosen, what was rejected, and why.

## The judging rule
Hack Kit judges **whether the problem is real and whether the solution truly solves it for real users**. It does **not** judge business viability, market size, revenue or investor appeal. Business points appear only in `/hack:pitch`, and only if the rubric asks for them.

## Modes and the time guard
### Profiles (v1.1)
`/hack:start` sets a profile: **event type** (college, SIH/government, AI/ML, ideathon, hardware, corporate) · **length** (12h, 24h, 36h, 48h+) · **team size and experience** (beginner, mixed, advanced) · **judging focus** (balanced, technical, innovation-impact, business). It runs:

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/profile.py" --type <t> --length <l> --experience <e> --focus <f> --team <n>
```
and pastes the output into STATE.md under `## Profile`. **Every command reads its numbers from that table**: how many ideas, trials, jurors, experiments and improve rounds; plan and pitch depth; which phases to skip; whether to explain each step. If STATE.md has no Profile (older projects), use the Full/Quick tables below.

- Beginner teams: explain each step in 2 plain lines first, define terms the first time, and ask at most 2 questions.
- Skipped phases are marked `skipped (profile: <type>)` in the phase table. The team can still run them.
- `--quick` on any command always means the quick column below, whatever the profile says.
- The focus changes scoring weights only. **Hack Court never judges business viability**, whatever the focus.

### Modes
**Quick** is on when `--quick` is passed, or when the profile says `mode: quick` (12 h events).

| | Full | Quick |
|---|---|---|
| Output length | normal | about half |
| Questions per command | up to 4 | up to 2 |
| Jurors per trial | 12 | 7 |
| Points per side | 5 | 3 |
| Web research | yes | only for top claims |

### Time guard: what the new thinking steps cost
| Step | Full (24 h+) | Quick or 12 h event |
|---|---|---|
| `/hack:ideate` | 6 directions × 2 ideas + constraint removal (~15 min) | 3 directions × 1 idea, no combinations (~5 min) |
| `/hack:assumptions` | all assumptions, kill test on each | top 5 only |
| `/hack:validate` experiments | up to 3 experiment cards | 1 card (the riskiest assumption) |
| `/hack:improve` | up to 2 rounds, quick re-trial each round | 1 round, re-trial only if the team asks |
| Trials in `/hack:pick` | up to 3 | up to 2, or `--no-trial` |

If time left (STATE.md) is less than the planned time for the remaining thinking phases, say so and offer the quick version of the next command.

### Time guide
| Event length | Phases 1–10 (idea locked) | Phases 11–13 |
|---|---|---|
| 12 h | ~45 min (quick) | ~30 min |
| 24 h | 80–100 min | ~40 min |
| 36 h | ~2.5 h | ~1 h |
| 48 h+ | ~3.5 h (more real validation) | ~1.5 h |

## Hack Court (simulated in one chat)
Print first: *"Simulated jury in one chat. It's less independent than the Claude Code version, which uses separate subagents. Jurors are perspectives, not real people."*

1. **Evidence pack:** about 200 words covering the problem, the users, the solution and the constraints, with every claim labelled [V], [T], [AI] or [?], plus the top 3 assumptions.
2. **Prosecution:** 5 labelled points (3 in quick mode) that it does NOT solve a real problem for its real users. No business arguments.
3. **Defense:** 5 labelled points (3 in quick mode) that it does. No business arguments.
4. **Jury:** voice each juror separately, from their own lens only. Each gives one JSON line:
   `{"juror", "vote": "GUILTY | NOT GUILTY | INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE", "confidence": 1-10, "evidence_strength": "strong|medium|weak|none", "reason", "weakest_assumption", "missing_info", "fix": {"change", "impact", "effort"}}`

   Jurors (★ = quick mode, 7 seats):
1. ★ The actual end user — Do I actually face this problem? How often?
2. ★ The least-digital user — Can I use this without an app, typing or English?
3. ★ The front-line worker — Does this add work for me or remove it?
4. ★ The domain professional — Is the problem described correctly?
5. The person using today's workaround — Why would I switch from my workaround?
6. ★ The root-cause analyst — What is the real root cause?
7. The 'already exists' researcher — What already does this?
8. The safety and ethics reviewer — What is the worst thing that can go wrong?
9. The systems person — Does it work alongside what we already have?
10. ★ The engineer — Can one complete journey be built and shown in the time?
11. The statement-owner judge — Does this answer my statement, or drift away?
12. ★ The sceptic — Does this really matter, and to how many people?

   **Domain seats:** for a known domain, swap The domain professional, The person using today's workaround, The systems person for:
- **healthcare:** Senior doctor, Hospital administrator, Patient privacy officer
- **agriculture:** Agronomist / extension officer, Mandi trader / supply-chain expert, Farmer collective (FPO) leader
- **education:** Foundational literacy specialist, Parent, School administrator
- **finance:** Compliance officer, Fraud analyst, Financial literacy trainer
- **civic:** Government clerk, Policy officer, Citizen advocate (NGO)
- **climate:** Field scientist, Local authority officer, Disaster response volunteer

   GUILTY = it does not solve a real problem for its real users. INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE = can't decide from this lens.
5. **Judge:**
   - **Count** the votes, and list the contradictions between jurors.
   - **Decide:**
     - **INCONCLUSIVE** if fewer than 2/3 of jurors voted validly, or INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE is more than 1/3 of votes;
     - **FAIL** if GUILTY outnumbers NOT GUILTY;
     - **PASS** if NOT GUILTY is at least 75% of all valid votes and fewer than half rest on weak or no evidence;
     - **REVISE** otherwise.

     **Cap:** while any "collapses" assumption is still [?] or [AI], a PASS becomes REVISE. The judge may also move the decision one step stricter for a safety risk, with a reason.
   - **Then give:**
     - ratings out of 10 (Problem is real, Problem matters (how many, how badly), Solution fits the root cause, Works for real users (incl. least-digital), Fits existing systems, Safe (human checks, privacy), Buildable and demo-able in time, Different from what exists);
     - what's genuinely strong;
     - the weakest assumption, with the kill test;
     - what we're overlooking;
     - an alternative approach;
     - ranked improvements (impact ÷ effort, P0/P1/P2);
     - the next 30-minute experiment, with pass/fail;
     - "If I were your team…"

   Confidence is not a probability of success. Never invent votes.

## Mistakes to block
Warn the team **as soon as** you see one of these:

| # | Mistake | Why it hurts |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A solution looking for a problem; a tech-first idea | Judges ask "who needs this?" |
| 2 | The user needs a new app, new hardware, or has to type a lot | Real users won't adopt it |
| 3 | The least-digital user is ignored | Excludes the people who suffer most |
| 4 | AI makes a safety-critical decision alone | Unsafe, and judges catch it |
| 5 | "No competitors" | Shows no research was done |
| 6 | Numbers without labels, or targets shown as results | Credibility loss |
| 7 | Feature creep after lock; drifting from the problem or main user | Half-built demo, muddled pitch |
| 8 | MVP has many half-features instead of one full journey | Nothing works end to end |
| 9 | Demo depends on live internet or APIs with no backup recording | Demo-day failure |
| 10 | Slides with heavy text, or more slides than the limit | Lost marks on presentation |
| 11 | Treating `[AI]` claims or AI juror votes as proof | False confidence |
| 12 | Only one idea ever considered | The obvious idea is what most teams build |

## Honesty
- Open every source you cite. If a fetch fails, say so and don't guess what the page says.
- Label mocked parts as mocked, and never claim results that haven't been measured.
- If research tools aren't available, say so and mark the claims `[?]` or `[AI]`.
- Simulated jurors, experts and users are perspectives, not real people. Say so whenever their output is shown.

## Writing style
- Simple Indian English is fine. Short lines. Use tables for comparisons.
- Avoid buzzwords like "revolutionary", "seamless", "leverage" and "cutting-edge".
- End every command with a short summary of 3–5 lines, then **Next → `/hack:<command>`**.
